active_paradigms.idea: Parametric integer search on the global makespan T with exact per-layer count feasibility (c[e] = max(1, ceil(w[e]/T)) plus optimal count redistribution), replacing the water-filling heuristic
active_paradigms.description: Instead of the heuristic T* = max(avg, max/denom), binary-search a single candidate peak load T. For a given T, per layer compute counts c[e] = clamp(ceil(w[e]/T), 1, ...) and check whether sum(c) <= num_phy; if sum < num_phy, distribute leftover replicas greedily by largest w/c reduction (this is guaranteed feasible since adding replicas only lowers loads); if sum > num_phy, T is infeasible. Binary search T over [sum/num_phy, max(w)] to ~1e-9 relative precision, then pack with the existing FFD bisection. This finds the true minimal achievable per-replica-load peak rather than a heuristic target, and the counts it produces are provably near-optimal for the makespan lower bound. Because the same T is used across all layers, the per-layer peaks are also jointly minimized, avoiding the current situation where refinement stops early when peaks[r] <= tl[r]*1.0001 with a suboptimal tl[r].
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Peak GPU load (load-balance quality) across all layers jointly
active_paradigms.cautions: Use relative tolerance (1e-9 * T) in the binary search to avoid infinite loops; clamp counts to at least 1 and at most num_phy - E + 1; keep the existing FFD packer as the placement backend since it already succeeded
active_paradigms.approach_type: parametric bisection on makespan with ceil-based count feasibility

active_paradigms.idea: Anytime steepest-descent local search on the joint (counts, placement) solution with a wall-clock budget, using best-of-random-restarts and ejection chains over GPU assignments
active_paradigms.description: Wrap the current pipeline in an anytime loop: maintain the best solution found; until a wall-clock budget (e.g., 60-70% of the 360s timeout) expires, repeatedly perturb the current best (randomly shift 2-4 replica counts between experts in random layers, or randomly reassign 3-6 items between GPUs in the packed layout), repack only the affected layers with FFD-bisection, and accept if the summed peak load improves (or with small simulated-annealing acceptance probability on non-improving moves early on). The key difference from the failed numpy local search is that moves operate on replica counts AND placements jointly with repacking, not just on a fixed assignment, and the acceptance uses the true objective (sum of per-layer peak GPU loads). Track total elapsed time with time.monotonic() and return the incumbent best immediately when the budget expires so runtime never blows the timeout.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Both score components: load balance via true-objective local search, runtime via strict time budgeting and incremental repacking of only affected layers
active_paradigms.cautions: Never exceed the timeout — check the clock every iteration; cache per-layer pack results keyed by (counts tuple) to avoid repacking unchanged layers; keep the deterministic baseline as the initial incumbent so the result is never worse than the current score
active_paradigms.approach_type: anytime simulated-annealing local search with time budget

active_paradigms.idea: Exact optimal single-layer packing via branch-and-bound / DP for the small-GPU regime, falling back to FFD when the instance is large
active_paradigms.description: In many evaluation configurations num_gpus and epg are small (e.g., 8 GPUs, a few experts per GPU), making exact makespan minimization tractable. Implement a depth-first branch-and-bound: sort items descending, assign each item to a GPU (branch only over GPUs with distinct current loads and non-full counts, symmetry-breaking), prune when current partial max load >= best found so far and when remaining total load makes the bound (max(current max, load of any GPU + remaining items that must go there)) infeasible. Use the FFD-bisection result as the initial upper bound so B&B only needs to close a tiny gap. For each layer, if items <= ~40 and num_gpus <= ~16, run B&B with a node cap (e.g., 50k nodes); otherwise keep FFD. This gives provably optimal per-layer peak loads in the common case, directly minimizing the evaluator's balance metric where the heuristic FFD leaves a small residual gap.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Per-layer peak GPU load (exact optimality in small instances), which is the dominant term of the balance score
active_paradigms.cautions: Strict node cap and time checks to bound runtime; symmetry-breaking is essential (skip GPUs with identical load+count state); memoize nothing across layers since loads differ; ensure the fallback path is byte-identical to the current successful FFD code
active_paradigms.approach_type: branch-and-bound exact bin packing with symmetry breaking

tried_paradigms.idea: Full-pairwise local search with numpy-vectorized neighborhood evaluation: after the existing pipeline, run a numpy-based steepest-descent local search over ALL (move expert replica to another GPU) and (swap two replicas across GPUs) moves, evaluated with vectorized delta computations instead of the current Python double loop
tried_paradigms.description: The current swap refinement in balanced_packing only compares the single heaviest pack against the single lightest pack with a pure-Python O(k^2) inner loop, and it stops at the first non-improving pair. Replace it with a numpy-vectorized full-neighborhood local search: represent loads as a numpy array, compute the delta matrix for moving any expert e to any GPU g in one broadcast operation (loads[g] + w[e] - current_load_of_e's_gpu), and for swaps compute the pairwise delta via outer products. Accept the best improving move (steepest descent) or all improving moves with a small tolerance, and iterate until no improvement or an iteration budget (~50 passes). This is a fundamentally stronger search (full neighborhood vs. heaviest/lightest only) while remaining fast because numpy does the O(n^2) delta evaluation in C. Apply it to both the group-to-node packing and the physical-expert-to-GPU packing stages.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: max pack load and load variance across GPUs — the direct evaluator metric — while keeping runtime low via vectorization
tried_paradigms.cautions: Maintain the cardinality invariant by only allowing moves that swap (not pure moves) when packs are full, or by pairing a move with a reverse move. Guard the iteration budget so the 360s timeout is never hit: measure per-pass time once and cap passes accordingly. Use float64 and a small epsilon (1e-12) to avoid cycling on ties. Keep the existing LPT output as the starting point so the result is never worse than the current score.

tried_paradigms.idea: Joint global replication + bin-packing via LPT with iterative peak-load reduction (flatten the hierarchy)
tried_paradigms.description: The current hierarchical approach (groups→nodes→GPUs) makes locally optimal decisions that propagate imbalance: replication counts are decided per-node before GPU packing is known, and group-to-node packing ignores intra-group variance. Replace the hierarchy with a single global two-phase loop: (1) compute replication counts for all logical experts per layer via the existing bisection water-filling on the FULL weight matrix (not per-node slices), giving per-replica loads w/cnt; (2) run one global LPT packing of all num_replicas physical experts onto num_gpus bins with the exact per-GPU capacity constraint num_replicas/num_gpus; (3) iterate: after packing, if max GPU load exceeds the water-filling target T, grant one extra replica to the expert on the peak GPU whose w/cnt reduction is largest, re-pack incrementally, repeat until no improvement or slot budget exhausted. This directly minimizes the true objective (max GPU load) rather than a proxy, and typically converges in a few dozen iterations. Keep the group/node constraints only as a tie-breaking preference (prefer placing replicas on the same node when loads are equal) so the hierarchical network locality is mostly preserved without sacrificing balance.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Max-GPU load (load balancing quality) primarily; runtime secondarily since incremental re-packing avoids full restarts.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Must respect num_physical_experts per GPU exactly (cardinality constraint); handle rows in batch but the peak-GPU selection needs the argmax across the whole layer; guard against infinite loops with an iteration cap; ensure logical_to_physical_map output format (X-sized third dim) matches the evaluator's expectations.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: greedy LPT with iterative water-filling refinement

tried_paradigms.idea: Local search / large-neighborhood swap on the final GPU assignment using scipy-style pairwise and cyclic moves
tried_paradigms.description: After any initial assignment (current hierarchical output is fine as a seed), run a local-search improvement pass directly on the true objective: for each layer, repeatedly (a) find the max-load GPU h and min-load GPU l; (b) search all single moves (move one physical expert from h to l if it reduces max(h_load, l_load) and preserves per-GPU counts via a simultaneous reverse move), all pairwise swaps between h and l, and small ejection chains (move expert a from h to l, move expert b from l to a third GPU m, move expert c from m to h); (c) apply the best improving move and continue until no improvement. Because per-GPU expert counts must remain equal (num_replicas/num_gpus), use swaps and 3-cycles as the atomic moves. This is a pure improvement operator on the actual metric and is orthogonal to how the seed was built, so it can stack on the current 0.127775 solution. Use numpy for O(1) load bookkeeping and maintain per-GPU item lists so each neighborhood scan is linear in items-per-GPU (~small), keeping runtime well under the timeout.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly reduces max GPU load and load variance per layer, which is what the evaluator scores; runtime bounded by iteration cap.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Cardinality per GPU must never change (only swaps/cycles allowed); replica ranks must stay consistent (a physical expert's rank travels with it); cap iterations (e.g., 200 passes per layer) to respect the time budget; verify no expert ends up duplicated on the same GPU in a way that breaks the physical_to_logical invariants.

tried_paradigms.idea: Balance across layers jointly using a shared replication-count LP relaxation solved with scipy.optimize.linprog
tried_paradigms.description: The current code treats each layer independently, but the evaluator aggregates over all layers; layers with skewed expert loads waste replication slots while other layers have slack. Formulate replication counts as a continuous optimization: variables c[e] >= 1 for each logical expert (shared or per-layer), constraints sum(c) <= num_replicas per layer, and minimize the maximum per-replica load T via constraints w[e]/c[e] <= T (linearize with c[e] >= w[e]/T). Solve with scipy.optimize.linprog (HiGHS) per layer — this gives the true optimal continuous relaxation of the water-filling target, then round counts with a knapsack-style rounding that preserves sum = num_replicas exactly (round down, then distribute remaining slots by largest fractional part, then re-verify the resulting discrete peak with one corrective pass). This replaces the 25-step bisection (which converges to a possibly suboptimal discrete solution) with an exact continuous optimum plus principled rounding. Additionally, if the evaluator's workload has multiple layers sharing the same weight statistics, share one LP solution across identical layers to cut runtime.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Optimal replication-count allocation (lower bound on achievable peak load), plus runtime reduction from exact LP vs 25 bisection iterations.
tried_paradigms.cautions: linprog needs the epigraph form: minimize T s.t. w[e] - T*c[e] <= 0 is bilinear — instead fix grid of T candidates and check feasibility sum(max(1, ceil(w/T))) <= num_phy, or solve the linearized version where T is fixed per candidate and only the count feasibility LP is solved; keep it batched/vectorized across layers to avoid thousands of LP calls; ensure integer counts after rounding sum exactly to num_replicas.

tried_paradigms.idea: Bisection-on-makespan bin packing with First-Fit-Decreasing feasibility check per layer
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of LPT + swap refinement, directly binary-search the minimal achievable peak GPU load T per layer. For a candidate T, split each logical expert's load into cnt[e] items of size w[e]/cnt[e] (using the existing water-fill counts), sort items descending, and run a First-Fit-Decreasing (or Best-Fit) packing into num_gpus bins each with capacity T and cardinality limit epg. If packing succeeds, lower T; if it fails, raise T. ~25 bisection iterations per layer give a near-optimal makespan directly targeting the metric, and FFD is O(n log n) per check so it is fast. Keep the best feasible layout found across the bisection as the final packing. This replaces the heuristic LPT assignment (which can leave 5-15% peak-load slack) with a direct search on the true objective.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: peak GPU load per layer (the balancing metric), and runtime (FFD checks are cheap)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Cardinality constraint epg must be enforced inside FFD (skip bins that are full). If no T in [avg, max] is feasible, fall back to LPT result. Use the water-fill target as the lower bound of the bisection to save iterations.

tried_paradigms.idea: Multi-start randomized LPT with best-of restarts and item-shuffle perturbation
tried_paradigms.description: Run the existing LPT packing K times (e.g., K=8-16) per layer with randomized tie-breaking: perturb item loads by tiny random noise (or shuffle equal-load items) so each restart produces a different packing, then keep the packing with the lowest peak GPU load. Randomized tie-breaking is the key lever because LPT placements of equal/near-equal items are arbitrary and the current deterministic version gets stuck in one configuration. Additionally include a few restarts where the smallest items are placed first (anti-LPT) to diversify. This is embarrassingly simple, vectorizable with torch tensors, and directly reduces peak load without any of the failed local-search machinery.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: peak GPU load consistency and quality across layers; runtime stays low since each restart is O(n log n)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Seed the RNG deterministically (torch.manual_seed) for reproducibility. Cap total restarts so runtime stays well within the 360s timeout; measure per-layer time and adapt K. Keep the swap-refinement pass only on the best restart's output.

tried_paradigms.idea: Joint replication-count optimization via makespan lower-bound matching: choose counts so per-replica loads are near-equal, then balanced round-robin placement
tried_paradigms.description: Reconsider the replication step itself: instead of water-filling on ceil(w/T), compute replica counts by targeting that every expert's per-replica load w[e]/c[e] is as close as possible to the ideal peak T* = max(sum(w)/num_phy, max(w)/ceil(num_phy/E)). Concretely, for each expert set c[e] = max(1, round(w[e]/T*)) and then fix the total via a single pass of marginal-gain adjustments (add to the expert with largest w/c - T*, remove from smallest excess). Then place items onto GPUs not by LPT but by a balanced round-robin: sort items descending and assign each item to the GPU with the fewest items among those with minimum current load (lexicographic tie-break), which enforces the epg cardinality constraint naturally and avoids the heap-full edge cases in the current code. This changes the count objective from 'fit under T' to 'equalize item sizes', which packs far more evenly when loads are skewed.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: per-replica load uniformity, which directly lowers achievable makespan; also removes fragile heap logic for speed
tried_paradigms.cautions: Must ensure sum(c) == num_phy exactly and every c[e] >= 1. Verify the round-robin never exceeds epg per GPU before the item list is exhausted; if it would, fall back to LPT for that layer. Keep the existing output tensor construction unchanged.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: marginal-gain count equalization + lexicographic balanced round-robin placement

tried_paradigms.idea: Simulated annealing with replica-count moves on the true peak-load objective
tried_paradigms.description: Replace the current deterministic 5-round refinement with a simulated annealing search over the joint space of (replica counts per layer, packing). The state is the logcnt tensor; moves are: (a) increment one expert's count and decrement another's in the same layer (preserving the num_phy total), (b) occasionally perturb the water-filling target T per layer. After each accepted move, re-pack only the affected layer with the existing FFD bisection (cheap, per-layer), and evaluate the true objective: sum over layers of peak GPU load. Use a geometric cooling schedule with a fixed iteration budget calibrated to the evaluation timeout (e.g., 30-60s total). Accept moves that worsen the objective with probability exp(-delta/temperature), where delta is normalized by the average expert load. Keep the best-ever state as the answer. This escapes the local optimum where the current greedy marginal-gain refinement gets stuck after one shift per layer.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary score via lower summed peak GPU load across layers (better load balancing), while staying within the runtime budget.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Per-layer re-packing must be fast; cache FFD results and only recompute the layer whose counts changed. Use a fixed wall-clock deadline check inside the annealing loop so the algorithm always returns within the evaluator timeout. Seed the annealer with the current water-filling solution so it is never worse than the baseline.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: custom simulated annealing (pure Python, no external library)

tried_paradigms.idea: Optimal per-layer packing via dynamic programming on small GPU counts / column generation with min-cost flow
tried_paradigms.description: The packing subproblem (assign items with loads and cardinality limit epg to num_gpus GPUs minimizing peak load) is the bottleneck. For the instances tested (typically 8-16 GPUs, epg ~ 8-16), formulate the feasibility question 'can all items be packed with peak <= T and at most epg per GPU?' as a min-cost max-flow problem: source -> item nodes (capacity 1 each) -> GPU nodes (edges exist for every item-GPU pair with cost 0) -> sink with per-GPU load capacity T and cardinality capacity epg. Feasibility with cardinality constraints and continuous load capacities is NOT a pure flow problem because item loads differ per GPU, but it can be solved with a flow formulation where each GPU node has two constraints; instead use scipy.sparse.csgraph or a direct min-cost-flow with scaled integer loads: quantize loads to integers (multiply by a scale factor, round), then feasibility becomes a bin-packing with cardinality limits solvable exactly by DP over GPU profiles when num_gpus is small. Binary search on T as now, but replace the FFD heuristic with the exact DP/flow feasibility check, giving provably minimal peak per layer for the chosen replica counts.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Peak GPU load per layer (the true objective), eliminating FFD's suboptimality gap on skewed distributions.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Quantization error must be bounded (use a scale factor so quantization is < 0.1% of the target). Runtime scales with num_gpus * epg * load range; cap the DP state space and fall back to FFD bisection if the instance is too large. Only apply the exact method when num_gpus * epg is below a threshold.

tried_paradigms.idea: Cross-layer replica-count redistribution using a global knapsack on redundant slots
tried_paradigms.description: The current algorithm fixes replica counts per layer independently (each layer gets exactly num_phy physical slots). Instead, treat the total redundant-slot budget across all layers jointly: compute, for each layer, the marginal decrease in that layer's achievable peak load as a function of the number of redundant slots allocated to it (a concave-ish curve obtained by running the water-filling + packing for a few candidate slot counts, e.g., num_phy-2, num_phy, num_phy+2). Then solve a small integer knapsack: distribute the total slot budget (sum over layers must equal L*num_phy) to minimize the sum of layer peaks. This exploits the fact that some layers have naturally balanced loads and waste redundant slots, while skewed layers are starved. Note: if the evaluator requires each layer to use exactly num_phy slots, reinterpret this as redistributing *effective* capacity by allowing layers to leave slots filled with cheap copies of the lightest expert while other layers get more replicas of heavy experts — check whether the evaluator permits per-layer count variation; if not, apply the same knapsack idea within the constraint by choosing which experts get replicated using a global priority queue across all layers rather than per-layer water-filling.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Summed peak GPU load across layers, by allocating replication capacity where it reduces peak the most.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Verify the evaluator's validity checks: if physical_to_logical_map must have exactly num_replicas entries per layer, the per-layer slot count is fixed and only the global priority-queue variant is valid. Build the marginal-gain curves with a small number of packing runs (3-5 per layer) to keep runtime bounded. Tie-breaking must be deterministic for reproducibility.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: custom greedy knapsack over marginal-gain curves (heapq, no external library)
